concept.name: Rolling z-score
concept.definition: The rolling z-score standardizes each observation of a series by the rolling mean and rolling standard deviation of its trailing window: how many recent-standard-deviations the current value sits from the recent mean. It converts levels into a locally normalized scale used by mean-reversion and Bollinger-style analyses.
concept.intuition: A z-score of +2 says 'today's value is unusually high compared with the recent past' — unusual measured in units of the recent volatility, not absolute price.
concept.mechanics: At each t compute z_t = (x_t − μ_t)/σ_t, where μ_t and σ_t are the rolling mean and rolling standard deviation over the trailing window of length w. pandas rolling().mean() and rolling().std() supply the components; care is needed on whether the current observation is included in the window.
concept.formula: z_t = (x_t − μ_t) / σ_t, with μ_t and σ_t the rolling mean and rolling standard deviation over the trailing window of length w.
concept.failure_modes: Z-scores assume approximate local normality and stationarity; in trending or fat-tailed series, |z| > 2 events are far more common than the Gaussian 5%, so 'extreme' readings are not reliable reversal signals. The statistic also inherits the window sensitivity of its mean and std components.
concept.misconceptions: A high z-score is not automatically an overbought signal — in a persistent trend, price can hold z > 2 for long stretches. The z-score is relative to an arbitrary lookback, not to any fundamental anchor.
concept.example: If the 20-day rolling mean of a spread is 1.20 with rolling std 0.15 and today's spread is 1.65, the z-score is (1.65 − 1.20)/0.15 = +3.0.
